genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a workshop supervisor uses two ways of teaching
the first one shows the movement and then has it copied
the second one lets the learner work it out alone before any correction
imitation gives clean results within the first week
what is picked up by imitation is poorly retained
working it out alone multiplies mistakes and wastes material
the learner who searched understands the reason behind every movement
faced with an unfamiliar task, the imitator stalls and the searcher adapts
the trainer blends the two approaches according to how dangerous the operation is
text: The workshop supervisor trains his apprentices two ways, and he never stops setting one against the other. The first runs on demonstration. He performs the movement in front of the learner, slows every stage down, then stands back and lets it be copied. The second, which he trusts more, makes the beginner fumble alone with the material before anyone corrects a thing. Demonstration pays off quickly, with clean work inside the first week, but the memory of it wears thin. Fumbling wrecks a good deal of stock and turns out one mistake after another, and yet whoever comes through it has grasped for good why every movement goes where it does. On an unfamiliar job the gap shows. The imitator, however careful, stalls, while the one who searched adapts. So the supervisor mixes the two, saving demonstration for the dangerous operations and free exploration for the assemblies that carry no risk.

units: the reviewer finds three strengths and two weaknesses in this beginner's manual
the notions are introduced in short linked stages
this progression keeps the reader from feeling out of his depth
difficult movements are broken down across several pictures
rival handbooks make do with one picture per movement
the author keeps away from obscure vocabulary while staying exact
the exercises offered are judged far too few
the answers at the back of the volume say nothing about the reasoning
the book is recommended to anyone who works in an orderly way
it suits badly the reader who needs to be corrected at every turn
text: Three strengths set this beginner's manual apart from comparable handbooks, and two weaknesses temper the praise. Its progression comes first. The book advances in short stages, each fresh notion resting on the one before it, so the reader takes in the material without ever feeling out of his depth. Its illustration comes next. Awkward movements are broken down across a run of pictures, where rival handbooks make do with a single one. Its language comes last, turning away from obscure vocabulary while conceding nothing in accuracy. The reservations bear on two points. The exercises closing each chapter remain far too few for anyone hoping to practice in earnest, and the answers, pushed to the back of the volume, keep silent about the reasoning that produced them. The book therefore suits an orderly reader, and suits much less the one who needs his errors caught at every turn.

units: the writer of the letter addresses his former trainer
he let a long stretch of time pass before writing
at the start he followed the instructions without grasping their sense
he said them over to himself from memory in the evening
the workshop then handed him a whole order
he ruined his first three pieces and thought of giving up
repairing the fourth piece showed him what patience was worth
he now lays out his equipment the night before and writes his mistakes down
he has been asked to train a newcomer
he finds that what he inherited above all is a way of looking at a mistake
text: I am writing at last, after letting far too long go by, to tell you what your teaching has become in my hands. At the start I followed your instructions without grasping any of them, and I said them over to myself in the evening like a lesson learned by heart. Then the workshop handed me an order of my own. I ruined the first three pieces and came close to walking away. It was while repairing the fourth that what you said about patience meant something at last. Now I lay my tools out the night before, I write my mistakes down in a notebook, and I read that notebook again before every fresh batch. Last season the manager asked me to break in a newcomer. I heard your own words coming out of my mouth, almost without choosing them. That is when I understood: what you handed me was a way of looking at a mistake, not only a trade.

units: explaining a notion to someone else improves retention
a lesson left sitting in a notebook demands no effort of memory
putting it into words out loud makes the brain hunt for every element
that effort of recall hardens the memory
an unexpected question brings out a gap nobody had noticed
a gap once noticed can then be filled
too wide a difference in level pushes the explainer to cut his account down too far
cutting it down that far warps what he thought he had a firm hold on
the ideal listener is slightly less advanced but able to push back
text: Do you hold on to something better once you have said it out loud to someone else? You do, and the reason is short. As long as the lesson sits in a notebook, nothing forces your memory to build it again. The moment you have to put it into words, your brain goes hunting for every link, and that hunt hardens the trace. And what if the other person asks something you never saw coming? So much the better. The question opens up a gap you would never have spotted on your own, and a gap you have spotted can be filled. Does that mean explaining anything to anybody pays off? No. When the difference in level runs too wide, whoever explains trims the whole account down too far, and that trimming ends up warping what he thought he had a firm hold on. So the right partner stands a step behind you, close enough to follow, fresh enough to push back.

units: the woman running a shared workshop describes a problem of keeping people
the newcomers were giving up after three sessions
they went home every evening with a botched piece of work
a volunteer craftsman saw the beginners tense up at their first cut
the team changed the way a session runs
a newcomer now finishes a piece that somebody else began
he takes care only of the finishing touches
the beginners leave with a finished object and they come back
the craftsman reckons that this choice slows down the learning of the cut
he grants that the learners stay long enough to end up learning it
text: The woman who runs the shared workshop made no secret of the trouble when we asked her about it. Beginners were dropping out after three sessions, she told us, because they went home every evening with a botched object in their hands. A volunteer carpenter, sitting over by the bench, backed her up. He had watched hands tighten at the very first cut. So the team rebuilt the way a session runs. Every newcomer now ends up on a piece somebody else began, she explained, with nothing left but the sanding and the smoothing. The beginner walks out holding a finished object, she added, and he turns up again the week after. The carpenter tempered all this a little. The arrangement slows down the learning of the cut, he said, but it keeps people around long enough that they end up learning it anyway.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge passed on by mouth and by hand before writing
spoken storytelling rested on the return of the same turns of phrase
the group put right whatever the teller got wrong
learning with the hands did almost without words
no rule in the abstract was taught to the beginner
the apprentice copied what he watched and was corrected on the spot
the right movement settled into muscle before it was understood
writing keeps the exact words but loses the voice and the presence
workshop teaching dies out if the craftsman trains nobody to follow him
the two ways of passing things on ended up completing each other
text: Long before writing froze what people knew, everything passed from mouth to hand, and that double road had laws of its own. Spoken story lived on repetition. The teller came back again and again to the same turns of phrase, and the memory of the listening group pulled him straight whenever he strayed. Handwork barely used speech at all. Nobody taught the beginner a rule in the abstract. He watched, he copied, he got his knuckles rapped, and the right movement settled into muscle long before it reached the mind. Once carved signs spread about, the comparison turned around. The written page kept the words untouched and lost the voice, the shading, the presence of the master. The workshop kept the movement alive and went dark with the craftsman who had trained nobody to follow him. In time the two roads came to answer each other.

units: the author describes four levers of lasting memory
going back over a notion at widening intervals fixes it better
a recall that comes a little hard hardens the memory
questioning yourself works better than reading again
reading again creates a misleading feeling of command
mixing exercises of different kinds slows the session down
that mixing teaches you to identify the problem before choosing the procedure
the brain replays the learned sequences during sleep
the most useful sequences move toward stable memory
these levers do not spare you repetition but make it pay better
text: Four mechanisms hold a piece of learning in place for good. The first is spacing. A notion gone over again at widening intervals settles deeper than the same notion drilled in one sitting, because every recall that comes a little hard hardens the trace. The second is self-testing. Questioning yourself beats reading the page again, since a second reading hands you a feeling of command that nothing checks. The third is interleaving. Alternating exercises of different kinds slows the session down, yet it trains you to name the problem before you pick the procedure for it. The fourth is sleep, during which the brain replays the sequences it has learned and moves the most useful ones into stable storage. Not one of these levers stands in for repeated practice. Each of them raises what that practice returns.

units: a beginner in bookbinding is given an instruction that strikes her as senseless
her trainer forbids her to sew before folding an enormous quantity of sheets
she carries out the order without believing in it
she feels she is losing a whole season
her folds grow even as the weeks go by
her fingers end up feeling the thickness of the paper without measuring
once allowed to sew, she gets a straight spine and clean seams
the trainer admits he went through the same ordeal and hated it
he explains that this dreary task trains the hand and not the craft itself
a hand already trained picks up the next movement easily
text: The apprentice bookbinder was given, in her first winter, an instruction that struck her as senseless. The master of the workshop forbade her to sew a single gathering until she had folded a mountain of sheets by hand. She carried out the order without believing in it, sure that she was throwing a whole season away. Week after week her folds grew even, and then her fingers gave up measuring altogether. They felt the thickness of the paper and stopped where they had to. When she was allowed to sew at last, she found the thread following a spine already straight, with no seam buckling anywhere. The master admitted then that he had gone through the same ordeal and had hated every hour of it. That dreary labor, he added, teaches nothing about binding. It trains the hand, and a hand already trained picks up the next movement without effort.

units: the procedure starts with cutting the piece into short fragments
an overloaded memory holds on to nothing
a fragment of two bars settles better than a full page
each fragment must first be played at a slow pace
a repeated mistake beds in as firmly as a correct movement
you join two fragments when one comes out clean three times running
the breakdowns happen above all at the joins between fragments
the session ends with a run through the whole thing however rough
the next day it is better to start from the joins than from the opening
ignoring this advice makes the beginning solid and the ending shaky
text: Start by cutting the piece into short segments, because a flooded memory holds on to nothing: two bars settle where a whole page melts away. Then work each segment through at a slow pace, since a mistake played over and over beds in as firmly as a correct movement, and going slowly keeps the fault from being written in. Once a segment comes out clean three times running, join it to the segment beside it, because a piece gives way at the joins far more often than in the middle of a phrase. Close the session with a run through the whole thing, rough as it may be, so that your memory keeps a trace of the shape as a whole. The next day, start from the joins and not from the opening. Skip that, and the first bars will gleam while the ending stays shaky right up to the concert itself.

units: a converted shed houses a neighborhood workshop
the people living nearby saw the retired craftsmen carrying their trade away
the young people of the area had nowhere to learn
an association set up a very plain arrangement
each retired volunteer puts in two half sessions a week
he takes on two beginners at the most
there is no program and no assessment
you start straight from a repair a neighbor has asked for
half of the beginners carry on from one season to the next
the old hands say that explaining forces them to pull apart their automatic movements
text: Sanding, sawing and loud talk fill the converted shed at the bottom of the street, home now to a workshop for the whole street. Everybody living nearby knew the problem. Craftsmen going into retirement carried their trade off with them, and the young people around here had nowhere to learn anything. An association put together an arrangement with nothing clever about it. Each retired volunteer turns up two afternoons a week and takes on two beginners, never more. No program, no assessment. You start straight from whatever a neighbor has asked for, a wobbly chair, a shutter that sticks, and the old hand shows you as the job goes along. Half the beginners carry on from one season to the next. The old hands gain something too, since explaining forces them to pull apart movements that had gone automatic.
